{{Short description|Method for computing topological features of a space at different spatial resolutions}}
{{hatnote|See [[homology (mathematics)|homology]] for an introduction to the notation.}}

In [[topological data analysis]], '''persistent homology''' is a method for computing topological features of a space at  different spatial resolutions. More persistent features are detected over a wide range of spatial scales and are deemed more likely to represent true features of the underlying space rather than artifacts of sampling, noise, or particular choice of parameters.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1090/S0273-0979-09-01249-X | title=Topology and data | date=2009 | last1=Carlsson | first1=Gunnar | journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society | volume=46 | issue=2 | pages=255–308 | doi-access=free }}</ref>

To find the persistent homology of a space, the space must first be represented as a [[simplicial complex]]. A distance function on the underlying space corresponds to a [[Filtration (mathematics)|filtration]] of the simplicial complex, that is a nested sequence of increasing subsets. One common method of doing this is via taking the sublevel filtration of the distance to a [[point cloud]], or equivalently, the [[offset filtration]] on the point cloud and taking its [[Nerve complex|nerve]] in order to get the simplicial filtration known as [[Čech complex|Čech]] filtration.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Kerber |first1=Michael |last2=Sharathkumar |first2=R. |date=2013 |editor-last=Cai |editor-first=Leizhen |editor2-last=Cheng |editor2-first=Siu-Wing |editor3-last=Lam |editor3-first=Tak-Wah |contribution=Approximate Čech Complex in Low and High Dimensions |title=Algorithms and Computation |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |volume=8283 |language=en |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |pages=666–676 |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-45030-3_62 |isbn=978-3-642-45030-3|s2cid=5770506 }}</ref> A similar construction uses a nested sequence of [[Vietoris–Rips complex]]es known as the [[Vietoris–Rips filtration]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dey |first1=Tamal K. |last2=Shi |first2=Dayu |last3=Wang |first3=Yusu |date=2019-01-30 |title=SimBa: An Efficient Tool for Approximating Rips-filtration Persistence via Simplicial Batch Collapse |journal=ACM Journal of Experimental Algorithmics |volume=24 |pages=1.5:1–1.5:16 |doi=10.1145/3284360 |s2cid=216028146 |issn=1084-6654|doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Definition ==

Formally, consider a [[real-valued function]] on a simplicial complex <math>f:K \rightarrow \mathbb{R}</math> that is non-decreasing on increasing sequences of faces, so <math>f(\sigma) \leq f(\tau)</math> whenever <math>\sigma</math> is a face of <math>\tau</math> in <math>K</math>. Then for every <math> a \in \mathbb{R}</math> the [[sublevel set]] <math>K_a=f^{-1}((-\infty, a])</math> is a subcomplex of ''K'', and the ordering of the values of <math>f</math> on the simplices in <math>K</math> (which is in practice always finite) induces an ordering on the sublevel complexes that defines a filtration
: <math> \emptyset = K_0 \subseteq K_1 \subseteq \cdots \subseteq K_n = K </math>
When <math> 0\leq i \leq j \leq n</math>, the [[inclusion map|inclusion]] <math>K_i \hookrightarrow K_j</math> induces a [[group homomorphism|homomorphism]] <math>f_p^{i,j}:H_p(K_i)\rightarrow H_p(K_j)</math> on the [[simplicial homology]] groups for each dimension <math>p</math>. The <math>p^\text{th}</math> '''persistent homology groups''' are the images of these homomorphisms, and the <math>p^\text{th}</math> '''[[Persistent Betti number|persistent Betti numbers]]''' <math> \beta_p^{i,j}</math> are the [[rank of a group|ranks]] of those groups.<ref>Edelsbrunner, H and Harer, J (2010). ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=MDXa6gFRZuIC&q=%22persistent+homology%22 Computational Topology: An Introduction]''. American Mathematical Society.</ref> Persistent Betti numbers for <math>p=0</math> coincide with
the [[size function]], a predecessor of persistent homology.<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00200823#page-1 | doi=10.1007/BF00200823 | title=On the use of size functions for shape analysis | year=1993 | last1=Verri | first1=A. | last2=Uras | first2=C. | last3=Frosini | first3=P. | last4=Ferri | first4=M. | journal=Biological Cybernetics | volume=70 | issue=2 | pages=99–107 | s2cid=39065932 | url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Any filtered complex over a field <math>F</math> can be brought by a linear transformation preserving the filtration to so called '''canonical form''', a canonically defined direct sum of filtered complexes of two types: one-dimensional complexes with trivial differential <math>d(e_{t_i})=0</math>  and two-dimensional complexes with trivial homology <math>d(e_{s_j+r_j})=e_{r_j}</math>.<ref name="Barannikov 1994"></ref>

A '''[[Persistence Module|persistence module]]''' over a [[partially ordered]] set <math>P</math> is a set of vector spaces <math>U_t</math> indexed by <math>P</math>, with a [[linear map]] <math>u_t^s: U_s \to U_t</math> whenever <math>s \leq t</math>, with <math>u_t^t</math> equal to the identity and <math>u_t^s \circ u_s^r = u^r_t</math> for <math>r \leq s \leq t</math>. Equivalently, we may consider it as a [[functor]] from <math>P</math> considered as a category to the category of vector spaces (or [[Module (mathematics)|<math>R</math>-modules]]). There is a classification of persistence modules over a field <math>F</math> indexed by <math>\mathbb{N}</math>: 
<math display="block">U \simeq  \bigoplus_i x^{t_i} \cdot F[x] \oplus \left(\bigoplus_j x^{r_j} \cdot (F[x]/(x^{s_j}\cdot F[x]))\right).</math>
Multiplication by <math>x</math> corresponds to moving forward one step in the persistence module. Intuitively, the free parts on the right side correspond to the homology generators that appear at filtration level <math>t_i</math> and never disappear, while the torsion parts correspond to those that appear at filtration level <math>r_j</math> and last for <math>s_j</math> steps of the filtration (or equivalently, disappear at filtration level <math>s_j+r_j</math>).<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Computing Persistent Homology|journal = [[Discrete & Computational Geometry]]|date = 2004-11-19|issn = 0179-5376|pages = 249–274|volume = 33|issue = 2|doi = 10.1007/s00454-004-1146-y|first1 = Afra|last1 = Zomorodian|first2 = Gunnar|last2 = Carlsson|doi-access = free}}</ref><ref name="Barannikov 1994">{{Cite journal|title = Framed Morse complex and its invariants |url = https://www.researchgate.net/publication/267672645 |journal = Advances in Soviet Mathematics | date = 1994|pages = 93–115|volume = 21|first = Sergey|last = Barannikov}}</ref>

Each of these two theorems allows us to uniquely represent the persistent homology of a filtered simplicial complex with a '''persistence barcode''' or '''persistence diagram'''. A barcode represents each persistent generator with a horizontal line beginning at the first filtration level where it appears, and ending at the filtration level where it disappears, while a persistence diagram plots a point for each generator with its x-coordinate the birth time and its y-coordinate the death time.
Equivalently the same data is represented by Barannikov's '''canonical form''',<ref name="Barannikov 1994"/> where each generator is represented by a segment connecting the birth and the death values plotted on separate lines for each   
<math>p</math>.

== Stability ==

Persistent homology is stable in a precise sense, which provides robustness against noise. The '''bottleneck distance''' is a natural metric on the space of persistence diagrams given by <math display="block">W_\infty(X,Y):= \inf_{\varphi: X \to Y} \sup_{x \in X} \Vert x-\varphi(x) \Vert_\infty,</math> where <math>\varphi</math> ranges over bijections. A small perturbation in the input filtration leads to a small perturbation of its persistence diagram in the bottleneck distance. For concreteness, consider a filtration on a space <math>X</math> homeomorphic to a simplicial complex determined by the sublevel sets of a continuous tame function <math>f:X\to \mathbb{R}</math>. The map <math>D</math> taking <math>f</math> to the persistence diagram of its <math>k</math>th homology is 1-[[Lipschitz map|Lipschitz]] with respect to the <math>\sup</math>-metric on functions and the bottleneck distance on persistence diagrams.
That is, <math>W_\infty(D(f),D(g)) \leq \lVert f-g \rVert_\infty</math>.<ref name=":17">{{Cite journal|title = Stability of Persistence Diagrams|journal = Discrete & Computational Geometry|date = 2006-12-12|issn = 0179-5376|pages = 103–120|volume = 37|issue = 1|doi = 10.1007/s00454-006-1276-5|first1 = David|last1 = Cohen-Steiner|first2 = Herbert|last2 = Edelsbrunner|first3 = John|last3 = Harer|doi-access = free}}</ref>

== Computation ==
The principal algorithm is based on the bringing of the filtered complex to its '''canonical form''' by upper-triangular matrices and runs in worst-case cubical complexity in the number of simplices.<ref name="Barannikov 1994"/> The fastest known algorithm for computing persistent homology runs in [[matrix multiplication]] time.<ref name="Morozov 2024">{{cite arXiv |last1=Morozov |first1=Dmitriy |last2=Skraba |first2=Primoz |title=Persistent (Co)Homology in Matrix Multiplication Time |date=2024 |class=math.AT |eprint=2412.02591 }}</ref>

Since the number of simplices is highly relevant for computation time, finding filtered simplicial complexes with few simplexes is an active research area. Several approaches have been proposed to reduce the number of simplices in a filtered simplicial complex in order to approximate persistent homology.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sheehy |first1=Donald R. |title=Linear-Size Approximations to the Vietoris–Rips Filtration |journal=Discrete & Computational Geometry |date=June 2013 |volume=49 |issue=4 |pages=778–796 |doi=10.1007/s00454-013-9513-1|arxiv=1203.6786 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Botnan |first1=Magnus Bakke |last2=Spreemann |first2=Gard |title=Approximating persistent homology in Euclidean space through collapses |journal=Applicable Algebra in Engineering, Communication and Computing |date=March 2015 |volume=26 |issue=1–2 |pages=73–101 |doi=10.1007/s00200-014-0247-y|arxiv=1403.0533 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Choudhary | first1 = Aruni | last2 = Kerber | first2 = Michael | last3 = Raghvendra | first3 = Sharath | doi = 10.1007/s41468-021-00072-4 | issue = 3 | journal = Journal of Applied and Computational Topology | mr = 4298670 | pages = 425–458 | title = Improved approximate Rips filtrations with shifted integer lattices and cubical complexes | volume = 5 | year = 2021| pmc = 8549989 }} Preliminary version at ESA 2017, {{doi|10.4230/LIPIcs.ESA.2017.28|doi-access=free}}.</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Brun |first1=Morten |last2=Blaser |first2=Nello |title=Sparse Dowker nerves |journal=Journal of Applied and Computational Topology |date=June 2019 |volume=3 |issue=1–2 |pages=1–28 |doi=10.1007/s41468-019-00028-9|doi-access=free |arxiv=1802.03655 }}</ref>

== Software ==

There are various software packages for computing persistence intervals of a finite filtration.<ref name="Otter Porter Tillmann Grindrod">{{cite journal | last1=Otter | first1=Nina | last2=Porter | first2=Mason A | last3=Tillmann | first3=Ulrike | last4=Grindrod | first4=Peter | last5=Harrington | first5=Heather |display-authors=3| title = A roadmap for the computation of persistent homology | journal = EPJ Data Science | publisher=Springer | volume=6 | issue=1 | date=2017-08-09 | issn=2193-1127 | doi=10.1140/epjds/s13688-017-0109-5 | page=17 | pmid=32025466 | pmc=6979512 |doi-access = free}}</ref>
